analysis.one_liner: Ends exclusive union representation, letting workers opt out of union contracts and dues in unionized workplaces.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: introduced with zero cosponsors, it sat in a House subcommittee until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law so a union no longer represents everyone in a unionized workplace. Employees who wanted union representation would have to sign up in writing, could revoke it at any time, and could never be required to join the union or pay dues or fees. Workers who opted out could negotiate their own deals with their employer, and a union contract would apply only to those who signed on. The bill was sponsored by Rep. Richard Armey with no cosponsors and died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees who object to paying union dues or being covered by a union contract could stop paying and opt out entirely, negotiating their own terms directly with their employer. Employers in unionized workplaces also gain: they could offer different pay and conditions to non-members, and unions would lose the fees and the bargaining position that come with representing an entire workforce.

how_it_helps.text: Would remove any requirement that individual employees join a union or pay dues or fees to a labor organization.
Would let employees opt out of union representation by revoking a written designation at any time, with no financial obligation after revocation.
Would let individual employees who do not opt in accept any other terms and conditions of employment they and their employer find mutually acceptable, rather than the union contract.
Would guarantee employees the right to bring grievances directly to their employer without going through the union.

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions would lose their fee base and their right to represent a whole workforce, making it much harder to finance and sustain collective bargaining. Workers in unionized workplaces would face weaker contracts, since employers could strike separate, lower-cost deals with anyone who opted out of the union agreement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions and workers in unionized workplaces

drawbacks.text: Union contracts would apply only to employees who affirmatively sign on, letting employers offer different terms to non-members and undercut the negotiated agreement worker by worker.
Unions would be required to represent only employees who affirmatively designate them, stripping away the dues and fee base that funds collective bargaining.

The bill offers no replacement structure for collective bargaining: if most workers in a shop opt out, the union contract effectively dissolves even if the workers had previously chosen union representation by majority vote.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that workers who never asked to leave the union but simply skipped signing up would get the benefit of union-won wages without the union having the resources to win them, a classic free-rider problem under this design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a real benefit to a narrow group: employees who object to dues or to union representation get to stop paying and bargain alone. But the mechanism goes far beyond that, converting collective bargaining from a majority-based system into an individually voluntary one. In workplaces where the union loses members and fees, contracts weaken and employers can cut separate deals with anyone who opts out. The cost falls on unions and on the unionized workers whose contracts the union exists to protect, and the bill provides no substitute for the bargaining power it eliminates.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Labor-Management Relations subcommittee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Armey introduced the bill on March 16, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No member of the House cosponsored it, from either party.
On April 5, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, where it remained with no further action.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, without the bill ever receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and workers in unionized workplaces, since the existing system of exclusive representation and negotiated contracts was left untouched. Employers who wanted the ability to opt workers out of union coverage did not get it this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Richard K. Armey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal exclusive representation and end mandatory union dues and fees; no member joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 5, 1993, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: William Ford
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee during the 103rd Congress; the bill never reached a markup or vote under his tenure.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no floor action, so no roll call shows the split; the only recorded support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: The bill would strip unions of exclusive representation and any right to collect dues or fees from employees who did not affirmatively sign up, cutting their funding and membership. Some employees would welcome not paying dues, but the resulting weaker contracts would cost workers generally, which is the union's core argument for the status quo.

Employers could negotiate individually with any employee who opted out of the union contract and offer different terms than the union agreement. That gain comes at the expense of the collective bargaining power of the workforce as a whole.
